title: Hydraulic Control of Fish Distribution at Large River Confluences: Evidence for Cross‐Sectional Flow Organization
content:
Abstract

Confluences are among the most hydrodynamically complex environments within fluvial networks and are widely recognized as ecological hotspots. Effective management of fish assemblages in such systems requires a mechanistic understanding of hydrodynamic-ecological coupling. However, existing studies largely emphasize macro-scale distribution patterns or integrated hydrological conditions, providing limited insight into fish utilization of three-dimensional flow structures at confluences. This study investigates hydrodynamic controls on fish spatial distribution and niche differentiation at the Yangtze-Poyang confluence, one of the world's largest confluence systems. During a biologically critical migration period, long-term field surveys were conducted across the mainstream, tributary, and post-confluence channels, integrating high-resolution velocity measurements with hydroacoustic fish detections. Results reveal that, despite pronounced longitudinal variability in hydrodynamic conditions at the confluence, consistent cross-sectional hydrodynamic zonation patterns persist across channels. These zones, jointly structured by water depth, flow velocity, and hydraulic complexity, comprise a high-velocity core, a shallow margin, and a deep thalweg. Hydrodynamic heterogeneity across zones exerts a stronger control on fish spatial distribution and niche structure than longitudinal variation among channel reaches. The deep thalweg functions as the primary habitat and longitudinal corridor supporting fish connectivity, whereas confluence-driven flow interactions substantially enhance fish utilization of the high-velocity core. Water depth acts as a consistent primary control across zones, while streamwise velocity exhibits zone-dependent threshold responses, with fish utilization peaking at intermediate velocities of approximately 40 ∼ 60 cm/s within the deep thalweg. These findings provide a process-based basis for understanding fish aggregation at large confluences and informing hydrodynamically grounded conservation.
